corrections.claimed_speedup: kostya/benchmarks (https://github.com/kostya/benchmarks), Chez Scheme 10.0.0, brainfuck bench.b: 1.758 s vs Node.js 2.954 s, Lua/luajit 5.686 s, Python/pypy 9.398 s (about 1.68x, 3.23x and 5.35x, derived from page data); Java 1.191 s is faster. mandel.b: 30.884 s vs luajit 31.804 s, Node.js 34.692 s, pypy 41.153 s (about 1.03x, 1.12x and 1.33x, derived from page data); Java 13.041 s is faster. Second source plb2 (https://github.com/attractivechaos/plb2, Chez 9.5.8, Apple M1): nqueen 3.54 s vs luajit 5.31 s, PyPy 6.91 s, Node 3.73 s and Java 3.92 s (faster than all four), but matmul 18.98 s vs luajit 2.66 s, Node 2.88 s, PyPy 4.89 s and Java 1.14 s (7.1x slower than LuaJIT and 16.6x slower than Java, derived from page data); plb2 has no Chez sudoku or bedcov.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: kostya: `scheme --optimize-level 3 --program` (common/commands.mk SCHEME_RUN), Chez Scheme 10.0.0 from the Debian chezscheme package; baselines luajit 2.1.1748495995, pypy 7.3.23, Node.js v26.5.0, Java 24.0.2, all run with default flags. plb2: src/scheme/run.sh uses the same `scheme --optimize-level 3 --program`, Chez 9.5.8.
corrections.caveats: Mixed results: Chez wins only the brainfuck interpreter tests in kostya (the only kostya tests that have a Chez row) and plb2 nqueen; plb2 matmul is 7-17x slower than every JIT baseline (its source stores doubles in a generic Scheme vector, so every element is a boxed flonum). The mandel.b margin over LuaJIT is about 3%. Java (HotSpot) beats Chez on both kostya brainfuck tests. optimize-level 3 is Chez's unsafe mode (type and bounds checks removed), which the baselines do not get. Chez is not a tracing or profiling JIT: the full compiler (Debian chezscheme package) compiles the program to native code when it is loaded, so the category fit is load-time compilation. The brainfuck programs differ in shape across languages (Chez walks a parsed op list recursively; LuaJIT's bf_jit.lua dispatches through one closure per op; Node, Java and C# use a parsed op tree with a switch), so the comparison is per idiomatic implementation, not identical code. plb2 numbers are from Chez 9.5.8 (early 2024 versions) and its author notes his non-C implementations may be suboptimal.

notes: All kostya and plb2 numbers verified on the pages; added that Chez also beats Java on plb2 nqueen and that the mandel.b win over LuaJIT is only 3%. Resolved the execution-mode question: the Docker image installs the full Debian chezscheme package and both suites run `scheme --optimize-level 3 --program` (compiled to native code at load, unsafe mode). tier_reason: kostya/benchmarks README rows match exactly; benchmark code brainfuck/bf.jl and matmul/matmul.jl is public, run via common/commands.mk JULIA_RUN (`julia --optimize=3 --check-bounds=no`), Julia v1.11.6 listed in the README environment, Intel Xeon E-2324G, baselines' versions and run commands in the same files. plb2 (Apple M1, versions in its table) agrees.

corrections.claimed_speedup: kostya/benchmarks (https://github.com/kostya/benchmarks), brainfuck bench.b: Julia 1.564 s vs Lua/luajit 5.686 s, Python/pypy 9.398 s, Node.js 2.954 s (about 3.6x, 6.0x and 1.9x, derived from page data); Java 1.191 s is faster. mandel.b: Julia 30.315 s vs luajit 31.804 s, Node.js 34.692 s, pypy 41.153 s; Java 13.041 s is faster. matmul 'Julia (no BLAS)': 1.113 s vs Java 3.057 s, Node.js 3.212 s, pypy 3.263 s (about 2.7x vs OpenJDK, derived from page data). Second source plb2 (https://github.com/attractivechaos/plb2, Apple M1): Julia 1.10.0 nqueen 3.02 s, matmul 0.76 s, sudoku 2.18 s, bedcov 1.96 s vs luajit 5.31/2.66/4.48/10.52 s, PyPy 7.3.14 6.91/4.89/8.82/6.27 s, Java 20.0.1 3.92/1.14/3.20/3.04 s, Node 21.5.0 3.73/2.88/3.77/2.45 s (faster than all four on all four tasks).
corrections.caveats: Workload specific: Java beats Julia on kostya's bench.b and mandel.b, and in kostya's other tests Julia loses to most baselines: base64 3.085 s vs Node.js 0.635 s and Java 1.435 s (Julia does beat PyPy 3.534 s there); primes 0.680 s vs Java 0.161 s, Node.js 0.207 s, luajit 0.309 s and PyPy 0.617 s; JSON (JSON3) 0.700 s vs Node.js 0.374 s, Java DSL-JSON 0.571 s and PyPy 0.606 s. In plb2 Julia beats all four baselines. The kostya run uses --check-bounds=no (bounds checks removed) and plb2's Julia sources use @inbounds in hot loops, which other languages' sources do not. The kostya 'no BLAS' matmul source is not a plain triple loop: it uses @simd ivdep and @fastmath (allowing reassociation and vectorized FMA, which Java and V8 cannot do) and wraps the outer loop in Threads.@threads (single-threaded here, since JULIA_RUN passes no -t and sets no JULIA_NUM_THREADS). Julia matmul rows at 0.12-0.17 s use BLAS and are not comparable. The kostya brainfuck bf.jl scans raw characters and brackets at run time, while the Node, Java and C# versions parse an op tree first, so the code shapes differ. Each program runs a small verify() before the timer starts, which warms the JIT on the same functions, so most compile time is outside the timed region; plb2 includes startup and compile time. kostya's docker/Dockerfile now pins julia-1.12.6 while the README environment lists v1.11.6, so the published numbers predate the current image.

notes: Every number in the claim matches the kostya and plb2 tables. Corrected one caveat (Julia beats PyPy on base64, it does not lose to it) and added that the kostya no-BLAS matmul uses @simd ivdep and @fastmath, so that row is not a like-for-like loop. corrections.claimed_speedup: JIT mode, kostya/benchmarks (https://github.com/kostya/benchmarks, .NET 10.0.100, Xeon E-2324G), 'C#/.NET Core' row: brainfuck bench.b 1.280 s vs Node.js 2.954 s, Lua/luajit 5.686 s, Python/pypy 9.398 s (about 2.3x, 4.4x and 7.3x, derived from page data); mandel.b 15.576 s vs luajit 31.804 s, Node.js 34.692 s, pypy 41.153 s (about 2.0x, 2.2x and 2.6x, derived from page data). Slower than Java 24.0.2 (HotSpot) on every kostya test it shares: bench.b 1.280 vs 1.191 s, mandel.b 15.576 vs 13.041 s, base64 2.374 vs 1.435 s, matmul 4.506 vs 3.057 s. NativeAOT mode, plb2 (https://github.com/attractivechaos/plb2, .NET 8.0.100 with PublishAot, Apple M1): nqueen 2.82, matmul 1.38, sudoku 1.62, bedcov 0.99 s vs OpenJDK 20.0.1 3.92, 1.14, 3.20, 3.04 s (faster on 3 of 4), luajit 5.31, 2.66, 4.48, 10.52 s and PyPy 7.3.14 6.91, 4.89, 8.82, 6.27 s (faster on all 4).
corrections.baseline: LuaJIT 2.1, PyPy 7.3.x and Node.js (V8) on kostya brainfuck in JIT mode; OpenJDK HotSpot only beaten in plb2 NativeAOT mode
corrections.compiler_and_flags: kostya (JIT mode): `dotnet build --nologo -v q -c Release` (common/commands.mk DOTNET_BUILD), net10.0 target, .NET SDK 10.0.100, default tiered JIT; baselines luajit 2.1.1748495995, pypy 7.3.23, Node.js v26.5.0, Java 24.0.2 run with default flags. plb2 (NativeAOT): `dotnet publish -c Release -r osx-arm64` (src/csharp/Makefile) with `<PublishAot>true</PublishAot>` in each of nqueen/matmul/sudoku/bedcov.csproj, .NET 8.0.100; Java, LuaJIT and PyPy invocations are not given in the plb2 README.

corrections.caveats: The plb2 .NET row is NativeAOT, not the CoreCLR RyuJIT JIT: every src/csharp/*.csproj sets PublishAot=true, which matches the AOT star in plb2's table (the earlier note that the mode was unclear was wrong). NativeAOT lives in the same dotnet/runtime repo and uses RyuJIT as its code generator, but those numbers compare an AOT build with JIT runtimes. In JIT mode (kostya) .NET beats LuaJIT, PyPy and Node.js on the brainfuck tests but is slower than Java (HotSpot) on all four shared tests, and on matmul (4.506 s) it is slower than Java 3.057 s, Node.js 3.212 s and PyPy 3.263 s; on base64 (2.374 s) it beats only PyPy (3.534 s), losing to Node.js 0.635 s and Java 1.435 s. The kostya JSON row (System.Text.Json 0.558 s vs Java DSL-JSON 0.571 s, PyPy 0.606 s, Node.js 0.374 s) measures libraries, not the JIT. The 'C# (Staged)/.NET Core' rows (0.373 s and 2.917 s) use a different staged-compilation program and are not comparable. The plb2 author notes that, being mostly a C programmer, his implementations in other languages may be suboptimal.

notes: Numbers in the original claim match plb2, but plb2 built .NET with PublishAot=true (NativeAOT), so they do not describe RyuJIT JIT mode; rewrote the claim to lead with kostya's JIT-mode results (A-level: code, flags, versions and CPU stated) and kept plb2 as the NativeAOT second source. Against HotSpot the JIT loses everywhere in kostya; the win is against LuaJIT, PyPy and V8 on interpreter-style code. Metadata verified: MIT, 18.3k stars, last commit 2026-10-06.
